questions.enonce_markdown:
What do you understand by the following terms:

(i) Peristalsis

(ii) Absorption

(iii) Assimilation

(iv) Egestion? *(7 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Peristalsis** is the **wave-like, rhythmic contraction and relaxation of the circular and longitudinal muscles of the wall of the alimentary canal**, which pushes the food forward along the gut.

(ii) **Absorption** is the **passage of digested food molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, vitamins, mineral salts and water) from the alimentary canal, mainly the ileum, into the blood or lymph**.

(iii) **Assimilation** is the **use of absorbed food substances by the body cells** to build new protoplasm (growth and repair), to release energy by respiration, or to be stored.

(iv) **Egestion** is the **removal of undigested and unabsorbed food material (faeces) from the body through the anus**.

questions.enonce_markdown: In what ways is the ileum adapted to carry out its function of absorption? *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The ileum is adapted for absorption in the following ways:

1. It is **very long and coiled**, which gives food a long time to be absorbed.
2. Its inner wall is **folded and bears numerous finger-like villi**, and the cells of the villi have **microvilli**, which give a **very large surface area** for absorption.
3. The wall of each villus and the epithelium are **only one cell thick**, so digested food diffuses a **short distance** into the blood.
4. Each villus has a **dense network of blood capillaries**, and the blood flow carries absorbed food away, which **maintains a steep concentration gradient**.
5. Each villus has a **lacteal (lymph vessel)** that absorbs fatty acids and glycerol.
6. The wall contains **muscle fibres** that move the villi and **goblet cells** that secrete mucus; the lining is **moist**, which helps dissolved food to pass through.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the digestion of food in the ileum. *(8 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Food enters the ileum as **acid chyme** from the stomach. Digestion in the ileum is completed by **three secretions**:

- **Bile** from the liver (stored in the gall bladder), which flows down the bile duct. It is **alkaline**: it **neutralises the acid chyme** and gives the medium the slightly alkaline pH (about 8) that the enzymes need. Bile contains **no enzyme**; its salts **emulsify fats** (break large fat globules into tiny droplets), giving a larger surface for lipase.
- **Pancreatic juice** from the pancreas, which contains **pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase**.
- **Intestinal juice** from glands in the wall of the ileum, which contains **maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases (erepsin) and lipase**.

| Food | Enzyme | Product |
|---|---|---|
| Starch | Pancreatic amylase | Maltose |
| Maltose | Maltase | Glucose |
| Sucrose | Sucrase | Glucose and fructose |
| Lactose | Lactase | Glucose and galactose |
| Proteins | Trypsin | Peptides (polypeptides) |
| Peptides | Peptidases (erepsin) | Amino acids |
| Emulsified fats | Lipase | Fatty acids and glycerol |

The end products (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) are then **absorbed** through the villi.
